The machine-to-machine archive pull takes the peer rail's transport decision: peer_secure_url and peer_tls_verify pin the house CA when the peer proves it, and only an unproven peer (no issued leaf) keeps the signed insecure fallback. The pinned peer signature authenticates the request.
legacy_reseal_peer_one mirrors the peer rail: a peer proved by its house-CA leaf is verified, and an unenrolled peer keeps the signed insecure fallback. The request carries the peer signature.

The git/APK/voice sync agent verifies against the house CA when peer_secure_url proves the peer; an unproven peer keeps the signed fallback so an unenrolled machine still syncs. The peer signature authenticates every request.

The reachability probe uses the transport each base's own listener proved: the verified house-CA listener is verified, and the plain manager port keeps the signed insecure fallback. The probe carries the signed claim.

music_source_uri decides whether the audio source is proved by its house-CA leaf; a proven source is verified and an unproven one keeps the signed insecure stream. The source signature authenticates the stream.

music_video_source_uri decides whether the video source is proved by its house-CA leaf; a proven source is verified and an unproven one keeps the signed insecure stream. The source signature authenticates the stream.

The remote auth/test path mirrors the peer rail: peer_secure_url and peer_tls_verify choose the transport, and an unproven listener keeps the signed insecure fallback. The request is signed by peer_sign_request.

peer_retry_useragent copies the caller's transport policy: when the original agent carries the house CA the fresh agent verifies too, and only a rail with no CA (a peer not yet issued a leaf) keeps the old lenient call so an unenrolled fleet still mints tickets.

remote_useragent_maker marks the agent insecure only when peer_secure_url did not verify the peer; a verified peer keeps the house CA. Both the cookie and no-cookie branches reach this same decision, so one entry covers the line in both places, and every request rides peer_sign_request.
key_push_one keeps the stored manager and the signed fallback for a peer with no house-CA leaf yet; the pushed key is what enrols it. Once the listener can prove the peer the same call is verified.

A raw homebase candidate with no remote_machines row has no CA to prove, so it keeps the signed insecure fallback; a recorded peer is verified through its house-CA leaf. The frame carries the peer signature and chip identity.

The remote-input HTTP fallback mirrors the peer rail: peer_secure_url and peer_tls_verify select the verified house-CA listener, and an unverified peer keeps the stored manager and the signed fallback.

A private-LAN device serves a self-signed leaf, so its own route keeps the lenient agent; the public house leaf is fetched by a separate agent on the system store. The LAN device is a known local appliance, not a remote peer.

An origin with no remote_machines row has no CA to pin (an unrecorded origin), so the cross-house profile lookup keeps the signed insecure fallback. A recorded origin is verified through peer_secure_url and the house CA.
The junderground client keeps insecure as an explicit opt-in setting, default off; the agent is lenient only when the person set it to yes. It is a deliberate user choice, never a default.

Reviewed design: tunnel_peer_enrol dials the hub's loopback tunnel port, which forwards to the peer's main/PORT_DOCK listener. That listener serves the peer's public wildcard or generated self-signed certificate; the house-CA leaf is on the peer listener (main port + 6), which this tunnel does not carry, so no CA held here can prove the hop. The signed /gate request authenticates the caller. Move the tunnel data plane to the peer listener to verify this later; until then this evidence pin keeps the lenient loopback rail.

Reviewed design: the device scan's gate call goes through the loopback tunnel (or the LAN manager port) to the peer's main/PORT_DOCK listener, which serves the public wildcard or generated self-signed certificate. The house-CA leaf is on the peer listener (main port + 6), which this scan does not dial, so it shares Tunnel.pm's trust limitation. The signed gate request is the proof here.

Reviewed design for both nearby_position and operator_door_push (their lines are identical, so one evidence pin covers both): the LAN target is resolved through peer_secure_url and peer_tls_verify, and the house-CA listener (port + 6) is taken only when its leaf proves the address. Otherwise the target's manager port keeps the signed lenient rail, because it serves the public wildcard or generated self-signed certificate that no CA held here can prove.

Reviewed design: the single lenient rail this route keeps in $lenient_post, for an unrostered house that holds only the generated self-signed certificate. A rostered peer uses peer_secure_url and the house-CA listener when its leaf proves the address; an unrostered public host is verified against the system store, and this lenient retry runs only after that verified request failed at TLS, so a fresh LAN house can still join.

Reviewed design: _hub_allow_self_signed is the peers-side fallback. A hub named by a public-looking domain uses the system store, and a loopback/LAN/tailnet name starts lenient because it may hold the generated self-signed certificate. A public-looking hub that nevertheless serves a self-signed certificate falls back here once, after the websocket callback reports a TLS failure.
